docs.title: How to cite
docs.text:
If ASymCat contributes to work you publish, please cite the software and the version you used. Results can change between versions (see the Changelog), so the version number is what lets a reader reproduce your numbers. Check it with:

import asymcat

print(asymcat.__version__)

docs.title: DOIs
docs.text:
Every release of ASymCat is archived on Zenodo with its own DOI:

  • A specific version: cite the DOI of the release you used, so readers get exactly that code. Version 0.9.0 is 10.5281/zenodo.23938358, and version 0.8.0 is 10.5281/zenodo.23917212. Other versions are listed under "Versions" on the Zenodo record.
  • All versions: 10.5281/zenodo.23917211 always resolves to the latest release. Use it when you refer to ASymCat in general rather than to results from a particular version.

docs.title: Citing the software
docs.text:
APA

Tresoldi, T. (2026). ASymCat: Asymmetric measures of association between categorical variables (Version 0.9.0) [Computer software]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23938358

BibTeX (biblatex, or any style that supports @software)

@software{tresoldi_asymcat,
  author  = {Tresoldi, Tiago},
  title   = {{ASymCat}: Asymmetric measures of association between
             categorical variables},
  year    = {2026},
  version = {0.9.0},
  doi     = {10.5281/zenodo.23938358},
  url     = {https://asymcat.tresoldi.org/}
}

BibTeX (classic styles without @software, such as plain or most journal templates)

@misc{tresoldi_asymcat,
  author       = {Tresoldi, Tiago},
  title        = {{ASymCat}: Asymmetric measures of association between
                  categorical variables},
  year         = {2026},
  note         = {Version 0.9.0},
  doi          = {10.5281/zenodo.23938358},
  howpublished = {\url{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23938358}}
}

Replace the version, year and DOI with those of the release you used. The citation metadata also lives in CITATION.cff; GitHub's Cite this repository button on the repository page builds APA and BibTeX entries from it.

docs.title: Citing the measures and their dependencies
docs.text:
ASymCat implements published measures. When a result depends on a specific one, such as Theil's U or the Chao–Shen entropy estimator, cite the measure's original paper as well as the software. The References page lists the source for each measure and provides them all as a BibTeX file.

ASymCat computes its smoothed probabilities and bias-corrected entropies with FreqProb. If those options matter to your results, cite FreqProb too; its How to cite page has the entries.

docs.title: Use of AI
docs.text: AI assistants helped with routine engineering and with reviewing the writing of this software and its documentation; the design, the data and the responsibility are ours. AI_USAGE.md describes how.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
ASymCat implements established association measures from statistics, information theory and computational linguistics. This page lists the primary source for each one, so that work using ASymCat can cite the measures as well as the software. All entries are also available as a BibTeX file: references.bib.

To cite ASymCat itself, see How to cite.

docs.title: Probabilistic measures
docs.text:
mle reports conditional probabilities estimated from the co-occurrence counts. With smoothing_method="laplace" or "lidstone", the estimates come from FreqProb (see Software).

  • Lidstone, G. J. (1920). Note on the general case of the Bayes–Laplace formula for inductive or a posteriori probabilities. Transactions of the Faculty of Actuaries, 8, 182–192. (Laplace and Lidstone smoothing)

docs.title: The Tresoldi measure
docs.text: tresoldi is specific to ASymCat; The Tresoldi measure gives its definition. It combines pointwise mutual information (Church & Hanks, 1990) with conditional probability.

docs.title: Resampling and multiple testing
docs.text:
permutation_pvalue shuffles the pairing of the two variables to estimate significance; bootstrap_ci resamples the co-occurrences to give percentile confidence intervals. Test significance and uncertainty controls the false discovery rate when testing many pairs.

  • Efron, B. (1979). Bootstrap methods: Another look at the jackknife. The Annals of Statistics, 7(1), 1–26. doi:10.1214/aos/1176344552
  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate: A practical and powerful approach to multiple testing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 57(1), 289–300. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1995.tb02031.x

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The reference is generated from the docstrings in the source, so it always matches the installed version. It is organised by module:

Module Contents asymcat.scorer.CatScorer The scorer: every association measure, smoothing, entropy estimation, permutation tests and bootstrap intervals asymcat.scorer functions Measures on raw series or tables, and helpers to scale, invert and reshape scores asymcat.common Reading data and collecting co-occurrences, n-grams, observations and contingency tables asymcat.correlation Association between two whole variables

The top-level package re-exports the names most often needed:

>>> import asymcat
>>> sorted(asymcat.__all__)
['CatScorer', 'build_ct', 'collect_alphabets', 'collect_cooccs', 'collect_ngrams', 'collect_observations', 'correlation', 'read_pa_matrix', 'read_sequences', 'scorer']

docs.title: asymcat.scorer.CatScorer
docs.text:
Class for computing categorical co-occurrence scores.

Initialization function.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cooccs List[Tuple[Any, Any]]

A list of co-occurrence tuples.

required smoothing_method str

Smoothing method for probability estimation. Options: 'mle', 'laplace', 'lidstone'. Default is 'mle'.

'mle' smoothing_alpha float

Additive constant for 'lidstone' smoothing (its gamma); 'laplace' always adds 1 and 'mle' adds nothing. Default is 1.0.

1.0 entropy_estimator str

Estimator for the entropies behind theil_u, cond_entropy, mutual_information and normalized_mutual_information. Options: 'plugin' (the maximum-likelihood estimate), 'chao_shen' and 'nsb' (bias-corrected estimators for undersampled data, from freqprob). Default is 'plugin'.

'plugin'

docs.title: mle
docs.text:
mle() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return an MLE scorer of conditional probabilities, computing it if necessary.

For every pair (x, y) the tuple is (P(y|x), P(x|y)): how well x predicts y, then how well y predicts x. This is the same X→Y, Y→X order as theil_u, cond_entropy and goodman_kruskal_lambda. With smoothing_method set to "laplace" or "lidstone", the probabilities are smoothed with freqprob.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (P(y|x), P(x|y)) tuples.

docs.title: get_smoothed_probabilities
docs.text:
get_smoothed_probabilities() -> dict[str, dict[Any, float]]

Return smoothed probability estimates using the configured freqprob method.

The joint distribution over all pairs of observed symbols is smoothed with the scorer's smoothing_method, and the marginal and conditional distributions are derived from it, so that they are consistent with each other.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[str, Dict[Any, float]]

Dictionary containing 'xy_given_y', 'yx_given_x' and 'joint', keyed by symbol pair, and 'marginal_x' and 'marginal_y', keyed by symbol.

docs.title: pmi_smoothed
docs.text:
pmi_smoothed(normalized: bool = False) -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a PMI scorer using freqprob smoothing for better numerical stability.

The probabilities come from get_smoothed_probabilities: the joint distribution smoothed with the scorer's smoothing_method, and the marginals derived from it. Use it with smoothing_method="laplace" or "lidstone"; with the default "mle", unobserved pairs get a near-zero probability and a very large negative score.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default normalized bool

Whether to return normalized PMI (NPMI) or standard PMI (default: False)

False

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

PMI scores for each pair (X→Y, Y→X)

docs.title: fisher
docs.text:
fisher() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Fisher Exact Odds Ratio scorer.

For each pair, this is the sample odds ratio (a * d) / (b * c) of the 2x2 contingency table, as returned by scipy.stats.fisher_exact. It is the unconditional maximum-likelihood estimate; R's fisher.test reports the conditional one, which differs slightly. A table with an empty cell gives an odds ratio of 0 or inf. Both tuple entries hold the same value; the p-values are given by fisher_pvalue.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (odds ratio, odds ratio) tuples.

docs.text:
fisher_pvalue() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return the p-values of Fisher's exact test.

This is the significance counterpart to fisher: for each pair it returns the (two-sided) p-value from scipy.stats.fisher_exact over the 2x2 contingency table. As with the other symmetric statistical tests, both tuple entries hold the same value.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

docs.title: theil_u
docs.text:
theil_u() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Theil's U uncertainty scorer.

For every pair (x, y) this computes Theil's U in both directions over the subset of co-occurrences where pair[0] == x or pair[1] == y, matching compute_theil_u(Y, X) and compute_theil_u(X, Y) on that subset. The underlying entropies are computed with a vectorized formulation (see _subset_entropy_components) that evaluates all pairs at once rather than re-filtering the co-occurrence list for each pair.

Entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator. Bias-corrected estimates are not confined to [0, 1]: a slightly negative value on a small subset means no detectable association.

docs.title: cond_entropy
docs.text:
cond_entropy() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a corrected conditional entropy scorer.

For every pair (x, y) this computes the conditional entropy in both directions over the subset of co-occurrences where pair[0] == x or pair[1] == y, matching conditional_entropy(Y, X) and conditional_entropy(X, Y) on that subset. The entropies come from the same computation as theil_u (see _subset_entropy_components) and follow the scorer's entropy_estimator.

docs.title: tresoldi
docs.text:
tresoldi() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Tresoldi scorer, the measure ASymCat provides for alignments.

For every pair (x, y) the tuple is (T(x→y), T(y→x)), with T(x→y) = sign(PMI) * |PMI(x, y)| ** (1 - P(y|x)): the PMI pulled towards ±1 as the conditional probability approaches 1. The conditional probabilities come from mle (so smoothing applies to them) and the PMI from pmi. See the documentation page "The Tresoldi measure" for its properties.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (T(x→y), T(y→x)) tuples.

docs.title: mutual_information
docs.text:
mutual_information() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Mutual Information scorer.

Computes MI(X;Y) and MI(Y;X) for each symbol pair, measuring the overall statistical dependence between the symbols. Entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator; bias-corrected estimates can be slightly negative on small subsets.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (MI(X;Y), MI(Y;X)) tuples.

docs.title: normalized_mutual_information
docs.text:
normalized_mutual_information() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Normalized Mutual Information scorer.

Computes NMI(X;Y) and NMI(Y;X) for each symbol pair, measuring the statistical dependence normalized by joint entropy (range [0,1] for the plug-in estimator). Entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (NMI(X;Y), NMI(Y;X)) tuples.

docs.text:
jaccard_index() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Jaccard Index scorer.

Computes the Jaccard similarity coefficient between the context sets of each symbol pair, measuring overlap in their distributions.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (J(contexts_x, contexts_y), J(contexts_y, contexts_x)) tuples.

docs.title: goodman_kruskal_lambda
docs.text:
goodman_kruskal_lambda() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Goodman-Kruskal Lambda scorer.

Computes λ(Y|X) and λ(X|Y) for each symbol pair, measuring the proportional reduction in error when predicting one variable from another. Like theil_u, it is computed on the subset of co-occurrences where pair[0] == x or pair[1] == y; when the predicted variable takes a single value in that subset, the score is 1.0, as for theil_u.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (λ(Y|X), λ(X|Y)) tuples.

docs.title: permutation_pvalue
docs.text:
permutation_pvalue(measure: str, n_permutations: int = 1000, alternative: str = 'greater', seed: int | None = None) -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Estimate permutation-based p-values for an association measure.

Unlike the parametric tests (chi2_pvalue, fisher_pvalue, log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue), this works for any per-pair association measure -- including the information-theoretic ones (PMI, mutual information, Theil's U, ...) that have no closed-form null distribution.

The null hypothesis is that the two variables are independent. A null distribution is built by repeatedly shuffling the pairing between the x and y elements of the co-occurrences (which preserves both marginal frequency distributions and the total count while destroying the joint association) and recomputing the measure. For each pair and direction, the p-value is the fraction of permutations whose score is at least as extreme as the observed one, using the (count + 1) / (n_permutations + 1) correction so the estimate is never exactly zero.

Because the co-occurrences are treated as exchangeable, sequences that expand into many correlated co-occurrences (e.g. n-gram collection) make this test slightly anti-conservative; interpret accordingly.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default measure str

Name of the association measure to test; must be one of RESAMPLABLE_MEASURES. It is computed with its default parameters.

required n_permutations int

Number of random permutations forming the null distribution (default: 1000). Larger values give finer-grained p-values (the smallest reportable p-value is 1 / (n_permutations + 1)).

1000 alternative str

Which tail to test, matching SciPy's convention:

  • "greater" (default): significant when the observed score is unusually high -- appropriate for measures where a larger value means stronger association (PMI, mutual information, Theil's U, chi-square, ...).
  • "less": significant when the observed score is unusually low -- appropriate for measures where a smaller value means stronger association (e.g. cond_entropy).
  • "two-sided": significant in either tail.
'greater' seed Optional[int]

Seed for the random number generator, for reproducible results (default: None, i.e. non-deterministic).

None

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (p_xy, p_yx) p-values, one per direction, aligned with the measure's own output.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If measure is not supported, alternative is invalid, or n_permutations is not a positive integer.

docs.title: bootstrap_ci
docs.text:
bootstrap_ci(measure: str, n_bootstrap: int = 1000, confidence_level: float = 0.95, seed: int | None = None) -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[tuple[float, float], tuple[float, float]]]

Estimate bootstrap confidence intervals for an association measure.

Whereas permutation_pvalue tests whether an association differs from independence, this quantifies the sampling uncertainty around the observed score. A bootstrap distribution is built by resampling the co-occurrences with replacement (n draws from the n observed pairs, preserving each pair's x/y link) and recomputing the measure; the confidence interval is taken as the percentile interval of that distribution, per pair and direction.

The point estimate itself is not returned -- obtain it from the measure method directly (e.g. scorer.theil_u()).

Because resampling can drop a rarely-seen symbol from a replicate, a pair may be absent from some replicates; such replicates simply do not contribute to that pair's interval. As with permutation_pvalue, co-occurrences are treated as exchangeable, so sequence data that expands into many correlated co-occurrences yields intervals that are somewhat too narrow.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default measure str

Name of the association measure; must be one of RESAMPLABLE_MEASURES. It is computed with its default parameters.

required n_bootstrap int

Number of bootstrap replicates (default: 1000).

1000 confidence_level float

Confidence level in the open interval (0, 1) (default: 0.95 for a 95% interval, i.e. the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles).

0.95 seed Optional[int]

Seed for the random number generator, for reproducible results (default: None, i.e. non-deterministic).

None

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[Tuple[float, float], Tuple[float, float]]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to ((xy_low, xy_high), (yx_low, yx_high)) -- a lower/upper bound for each direction, aligned with the measure's own output.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If measure is not supported, confidence_level is not in (0, 1), or n_bootstrap is not a positive integer.

docs.title: collect_observations
docs.text:
collect_observations(cooccs: list[tuple]) -> dict

Build a dictionary of observations for all possible correspondences.

The counts of observations are derived from typical organization in a non-squared contingency table, using indexes 0, 1, and 2, where 0 means that the identity is not considered (so that "00" would refer to all correspondence pairs), 1 that there is a match, and 2 that there is a mismatch. In more detail, given a pair of symbols x and y, the counts of co-occurrences will be:

  • obs["10"]: number of pairs matching x (with any y)
  • obs["20"]: number of pairs not matching x (with any y)
  • obs["01"]: number of pairs matching y (with any x)
  • obs["02"]: number of pairs not matching y (with any x)
  • obs["11"]: number of pairs matching x and matching y
  • obs["12"]: number of pairs matching x and not matching y
  • obs["21"]: number of pairs not matching x and matching y
  • obs["22"]: number of pairs not matching x and matching Y

Note that obs["22"] is not the number of pairs where either x or y are mismatching, but where both necessarily mismatch.

When doing x->y, a non-squared contingency table will be

|            |  pair[1]  | pair[1]==y | pair[1]!=y |
| pair[0]==x | obs["10"] | obs["11"]  | obs["12"]  |
| pair[0]!=x | obs["20"] | obs["21"]  | obs["22"]  |

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default cooccs List[tuple]

A list of tuples of co-occurring elements.

required

Returns:

Name Type Description obs dict

A dictionary of observations per co-occurrence type.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If cooccs is empty or contains invalid tuples.

TypeError

If cooccs is not a list.

docs.text:
Association between two whole variables, given as aligned series. See Summarise whole variables.

Convenience wrappers for computing association measures on parallel series.

Unlike asymcat.scorer.CatScorer, which returns per-symbol-pair directional scores from a list of co-occurrences, the helpers in this module operate on two aligned series (series_x and series_y) and return a single summary statistic for the pair of variables.

docs.title: Choosing a measure
docs.text:
Start from the question you want to answer. The table gives the measures that answer it, and the notes below help choose among them.

Question Measures How likely is \(y\) when \(x\) occurs? mle How much does knowing \(x\) tell me about \(y\), beyond its base rate? theil_u, cond_entropy How many fewer prediction errors does knowing \(x\) give? goodman_kruskal_lambda Do \(x\) and \(y\) co-occur more, or less, than chance predicts? pmi (signed), fisher odds ratio Is the association statistically significant? fisher_pvalue, chi2_pvalue, log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue; permutation_pvalue for any measure How strong is the association, on a fixed scale? cramers_v, normalized_mutual_information, NPMI How much do the occurrences of \(x\) and \(y\) overlap? jaccard_index How should symbols in an alignment be scored? tresoldi

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
Start with mle and theil_u. The conditional probability is the easiest to read and to check by hand; Theil's U adds a correction for the base rate, so a frequent \(y\) does not look predictable from every \(x\). Disagreement between them usually means that \(y\) is frequent.

Use a signed measure to tell attraction from avoidance. The measures on the pair subset (Theil's U, conditional entropy, mutual information, λ) and the test statistics are unsigned: a pair that never co-occurs can score as high as one that always does. Check the sign of PMI, or the conditional probability, before interpreting a high score. See Pitfalls.

Prefer exact or resampling tests for sparse data. With small counts, chi-square and G² rely on an approximation that does not hold; use Fisher's exact test for the 2×2 table, or permutation_pvalue for any measure. See Test significance and uncertainty.

Smooth or correct when counts are small. Laplace or Lidstone smoothing stabilizes the conditional probabilities and pmi_smoothed; the Chao–Shen and NSB estimators reduce the bias of the information-theoretic measures. See Work with sparse data.

Compare scores within a dataset. PMI, G² and the conditional entropy depend on the sample size or the number of symbols. To compare across datasets, prefer a bounded measure (Theil's U, Cramér's V, NMI) and report the sample sizes.

docs.title: One number hides the direction
docs.text:
Most measures of association report one number for a pair of variables, as if the relationship between \(X\) and \(Y\) were the same as between \(Y\) and \(X\). Many real relationships are not. In English spelling, the letter q is always pronounced /k/, but /k/ is usually spelled some other way: q predicts /k/ perfectly, while /k/ hardly predicts q. A symmetric measure averages the two and reports a moderate association, which describes neither direction.

ASymCat therefore scores every pair in both directions. For a pair \((x, y)\), each measure returns a tuple

\[ \big(\text{score}(x \to y),\ \text{score}(y \to x)\big), \]

where \(x \to y\) reads "\(x\) as a predictor of \(y\)".

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> k_given_q, q_given_k = CatScorer(pairs).mle()[("q", "k")]
>>> round(k_given_q, 2), round(q_given_k, 2)
(1.0, 0.18)

docs.title: Directional and symmetric measures
docs.text:
The measures fall into two groups. Directional measures can give different values in the two positions of the tuple. Symmetric measures are the same in both directions by definition, so the tuple repeats one value; ASymCat returns them in the same format so that every measure can be used the same way.

Directional Symmetric mle, theil_u, cond_entropy, goodman_kruskal_lambda, tresoldi pmi, pmi_smoothed, mutual_information, normalized_mutual_information, chi2, cramers_v, fisher, log_likelihood_ratio, jaccard_index

The symmetric measures remain useful alongside the directional ones: they say whether a pair departs from independence at all (PMI, the statistical tests), and the directional measures then say which way the prediction runs.

docs.title: Where asymmetry comes from
docs.text:
For the conditional probability, the two directions share a numerator and differ in the denominator:

\[ P(y \mid x) = \frac{c(x, y)}{c(x)}, \qquad P(x \mid y) = \frac{c(x, y)}{c(y)}. \]

They differ whenever \(x\) and \(y\) have different frequencies. Theil's U behaves in the same way: both directions share the mutual information and divide it by the entropy of a different variable. Asymmetry is therefore not a property of a pair alone, but of the pair within its data: a symbol that occurs with many partners is a poor predictor of any one of them, even when each of them predicts it well.

docs.title: What the direction does not mean
docs.text: The direction of a score refers to which variable is conditioned on, not to time or cause. "\(x\) predicts \(y\)" means that knowing \(x\) narrows down \(y\), as the letter narrows down the sound. Whether one causes the other is a question about how the data came about, which association measures cannot answer.

docs.title: Pairs and whole variables
docs.text: CatScorer scores pairs of values: q with /k/, c with /s/. To summarise the association between two whole variables (all letters against all sounds) with one number in each direction, use the functions in asymcat.correlation (see Summarise whole variables).

docs.title: Notation
docs.text: This page fixes the notation used across the documentation and the example data that the measure pages share.

docs.title: Co-occurrences
docs.text:
ASymCat works on a list of co-occurrences: pairs \((x, y)\) in which \(x\) comes from one categorical variable and \(y\) from another. The two variables need not share values. In the example below, \(x\) is a letter and \(y\) is a sound.

Symbol Meaning \(\mathcal{X}\), \(\mathcal{Y}\) the alphabets: the distinct values observed for each variable \(n\) the number of co-occurrences \(c(x, y)\) the number of co-occurrences of \(x\) with \(y\) \(c(x)\), \(c(y)\) the number of co-occurrences whose first element is \(x\), or whose second element is \(y\) \(P(x, y)\), \(P(x)\), \(P(y)\) relative frequencies: \(c(x, y)/n\), \(c(x)/n\) and \(c(y)/n\) \(P(y \mid x)\) the conditional probability \(c(x, y)/c(x)\), and likewise \(P(x \mid y) = c(x, y)/c(y)\) \(H(\cdot)\), \(I(\cdot\,;\cdot)\) entropy and mutual information, in nats (natural logarithms)

docs.title: The score tuple
docs.text:
Every measure is a method of CatScorer that returns a dictionary. It has an entry for every pair in \(\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}\), including pairs that were never observed together, and each value is a tuple

\[ \big(\text{score}(x \to y),\ \text{score}(y \to x)\big). \]

The first number scores \(x\) as a predictor of \(y\); the second scores \(y\) as a predictor of \(x\). For the conditional probability, the tuple is \(\big(P(y \mid x),\ P(x \mid y)\big)\). Several measures are symmetric by definition and repeat one value in both positions; see Directional association.

docs.title: The example data
docs.text:
The measure pages use the same small dataset: how English spellings map to sounds. The letter q is always pronounced /k/, while /k/ is spelled c, k or q, and c can also be /s/.

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> scorer.alphabet_x, scorer.alphabet_y
(['c', 'k', 'q'], ['k', 's'])
>>> len(pairs)
15

Arranged as a table of counts \(c(x, y)\):

/k/ /s/ \(c(x)\) c 6 4 10 k 3 0 3 q 2 0 2 \(c(y)\) 11 4 \(n = 15\)

docs.title: Two views of a pair
docs.text: Measures look at a pair \((x, y)\) in one of two ways.

docs.title: The 2×2 contingency table
docs.text:
The statistical measures (chi-square, Cramér's V, Fisher's exact test and the log-likelihood ratio) classify all \(n\) co-occurrences by whether their first element is \(x\) and whether their second element is \(y\):

\(y\) not \(y\) \(x\) \(c(x, y)\) \(c(x) - c(x, y)\) not \(x\) \(c(y) - c(x, y)\) \(n - c(x) - c(y) + c(x, y)\)

For c and /k/:

>>> from asymcat.common import build_ct
>>> build_ct(scorer.obs[("c", "k")])
[[6, 4], [5, 0]]

These measures also accept square_ct=False, which is deprecated: it uses the 2×3 table that build_ct(..., square=False) returns, which adds the row totals \(c(x)\) and \(n - c(x)\) as a first column and is not a contingency table of the pair.

docs.title: The pair subset
docs.text:
The information-theoretic measures (Theil's U, conditional entropy, mutual information) and Goodman–Kruskal λ are computed on the pair subset \(S(x, y)\): the co-occurrences whose first element is \(x\) or whose second element is \(y\). In the table of counts, this is the row of \(x\) and the column of \(y\). Within the subset, the first and second elements are treated as two random variables, \(X_S\) and \(Y_S\), and the measure is computed for them.

For c and /k/, the row of c (10 pairs) and the column of /k/ (11 pairs) share the 6 pairs of c with /k/, so \(|S| = 10 + 11 - 6 = 15\): here the subset is the whole dataset. For q and /k/, the row of q lies inside the column of /k/, so the subset is that column: 11 pairs, all with \(y =\) /k/.

The pair subset makes these measures local to the pair, but it also has consequences that the Pitfalls page explains: in a subset where one variable takes a single value, its entropy is zero, and measures fall back on a convention.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
Association measures are easy to compute and easy to misread. This page collects the surprises that come up most often, with the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)

docs.title: Symmetric measures return two equal numbers
docs.text:
Every measure returns a tuple \((x \to y,\ y \to x)\), but only some measures are directional. PMI, mutual information, the statistical tests and the Jaccard index repeat one value:

>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.pmi()[("c", "s")]]
[0.405, 0.405]

Equal values from a symmetric measure say nothing about the symmetry of the relationship. Directional association lists which measures are which.

docs.title: High scores can mean avoidance
docs.text:
The information-theoretic measures and Goodman–Kruskal λ are computed on the pair subset and measure predictability, whatever its source. k and /s/ never occur together, yet:

>>> scorer.theil_u()[("k", "s")]
(1.0, 1.0)
>>> scorer.mle()[("k", "s")]
(0.0, 0.0)

In their subset, k is always /k/ and /s/ is always c, so each variable predicts the other perfectly: the pair is perfectly predictable because the two symbols exclude each other. Before reading a high Theil's U, mutual information or λ as attraction, check the sign of the PMI or the conditional probability. The test statistics (chi-square, G²) are unsigned in the same way.

docs.title: Degenerate subsets fall back on conventions
docs.text:
When one variable takes a single value in the pair subset, there is nothing left to predict, and the measures fall back on a convention: Theil's U and λ score that direction as 1.

>>> [round(u, 3) for u in scorer.theil_u()[("q", "k")]]
[1.0, 0.0]
>>> scorer.goodman_kruskal_lambda()[("q", "k")]
(1.0, 0.0)

In the subset of q and /k/, the sound is always /k/, so knowing the letter predicts it trivially. The 1 is not evidence about q in particular. Pairs whose subset is small or degenerate are best judged with the conditional probability and its count.

docs.title: Unobserved pairs are scored too
docs.text:
Each measure returns every pair in \(\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}\), including pairs that never co-occur. Their scores come from conventions rather than evidence: 0 for the conditional probability, a floor of \((1/n)^2\) for the joint probability in PMI, and 0 or \(\infty\) for the odds ratio. Filter them with scorer.obs[pair]["11"] > 0 when only observed pairs matter.

>>> observed = [pair for pair in scorer.obs if scorer.obs[pair]["11"] > 0]
>>> sorted(observed)
[('c', 'k'), ('c', 's'), ('k', 'k'), ('q', 'k')]

docs.title: Infinite values break scaling
docs.text:
Fisher's odds ratio is \(\infty\) or 0 whenever a cell of the 2×2 table is empty, which is common with categorical data. Scaling a scorer that holds an infinite value produces nan:

>>> from asymcat.scorer import scale_scorer
>>> scorer.fisher()[("c", "s")]
(inf, inf)
>>> scale_scorer(scorer.fisher())[("c", "s")]
(nan, nan)

Rank such measures directly, or use their p-values.

docs.title: Small samples and the chi-square approximation
docs.text:
The \(\chi^2\) and \(G^2\) p-values rely on a large-sample approximation. With few co-occurrences they disagree with each other and with the exact test:

>>> round(scorer.chi2_pvalue()[("c", "k")][0], 2)
0.3
>>> round(scorer.log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue()[("c", "k")][0], 2)
0.05
>>> round(scorer.fisher_pvalue()[("c", "k")][0], 2)
0.23

chi2 uses Yates' continuity correction, which makes it conservative; G² has no correction. Use Fisher's exact test, or a permutation test, when counts are small. The bias-corrected Cramér's V is 0 here for every pair: on 15 co-occurrences, no association exceeds what chance would produce.

docs.title: Negative zeros and small negative values
docs.text: Entropy differences computed in floating point can come out as -0.0 or as a tiny negative number where the exact value is 0. With the bias-corrected entropy estimators (entropy_estimator="chao_shen" or "nsb"), Theil's U and mutual information can also be slightly negative on small subsets; this means no detectable association, not a negative one.

docs.title: Collecting from sequences multiplies the evidence
docs.text:
collect_cooccs without an order pairs every element of one sequence with every element of the other, so a pair of words of length 5 contributes 25 co-occurrences. This is appropriate when position does not matter, as in two lists of attributes of the same item, but for aligned sequences use order=1, which pairs elements position by position.

In both cases, the co-occurrences from one sequence pair are not independent observations. The statistical tests and the resampling tools treat them as exchangeable, so their p-values are somewhat too small, and their confidence intervals too narrow, when sequences are long.

docs.title: pmi_smoothed with the default smoothing
docs.text:
pmi_smoothed estimates the probabilities with the scorer's smoothing_method. With the default, "mle", there is no smoothing, and unobserved pairs get a near-zero probability from FreqProb and a very large negative score:

>>> round(scorer.pmi_smoothed()[("q", "s")][0])
-20

Create the scorer with smoothing_method="laplace" or "lidstone" to use it (see Work with sparse data).

docs.title: Direction is not causation
docs.text: "\(x \to y\)" means that \(x\) is used to predict \(y\). Both directions are computed from the same co-occurrence counts, and neither says anything about which variable comes first or influences the other.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
ASymCat supports Python 3.10 to 3.12 and installs from PyPI:

pip install asymcat

It depends only on FreqProb, NumPy and SciPy. The plotting examples in this documentation also use matplotlib, which the viz extra installs together with seaborn and pandas:

pip install "asymcat[viz]"

To check the installation and the version:

>>> import asymcat
>>> isinstance(asymcat.__version__, str)
True

Report the version when you cite ASymCat: results can change between versions, as the Changelog and the Migration guide explain.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
To work on ASymCat itself, clone the repository and install it in editable mode with the development tools:

git clone https://github.com/tresoldi/asymcat.git
cd asymcat
pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest

The repository also ships sample datasets in resources/, with their sources and licences.

Next: the Tutorial.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial goes from a list of observations to directional scores, tests and matrices ready to plot. It takes about ten minutes, and every example can be pasted into a Python session. The examples use English spelling and pronunciation, but nothing in ASymCat is specific to language: any two categorical variables observed together will do.

docs.title: Score pairs of observations
docs.text:
ASymCat starts from co-occurrences: pairs \((x, y)\) of values observed together. Here, each pair is a letter and the sound it spells:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)

A CatScorer computes every measure from these pairs, on demand. The simplest is the conditional probability:

>>> mle = scorer.mle()
>>> k_given_q, q_given_k = mle[("q", "k")]
>>> round(k_given_q, 2), round(q_given_k, 2)
(1.0, 0.18)

Every measure returns a dictionary from pairs \((x, y)\) to tuples \((x \to y,\ y \to x)\). Here, q predicts /k/ perfectly, while /k/ points back to q only 18% of the time: the association is directional. A symmetric measure would report one number and hide that difference.

The dictionary covers every combination of the observed values, including pairs never seen together:

>>> sorted(mle)
[('c', 'k'), ('c', 's'), ('k', 'k'), ('k', 's'), ('q', 'k'), ('q', 's')]
>>> mle[("q", "s")]
(0.0, 0.0)

docs.title: Compare measures
docs.text:
Measures answer different questions (see Choosing a measure). For c and /k/:

>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.mle()[("c", "k")]]
[0.6, 0.545]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.theil_u()[("c", "k")]]
[0.226, 0.152]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.pmi()[("c", "k")]]
[-0.201, -0.201]

c is /k/ six times in ten, and knowing the letter removes 23% of the uncertainty about the sound (Theil's U). Yet the PMI is negative: /k/ is so frequent that c is pronounced /k/ slightly less often than chance would predict, because c is also the only spelling of /s/. Each measure page explains what its numbers mean.

docs.title: Collect co-occurrences from sequences
docs.text:
Data often comes as pairs of sequences, such as words and their pronunciations. collect_cooccs turns aligned sequences into co-occurrences, position by position with order=1:

>>> import asymcat
>>> words = [("cat", "kat"), ("cot", "kot"), ("city", "siti"), ("kit", "kit"), ("cent", "sent")]
>>> cooccs = asymcat.collect_cooccs(words, order=1)
>>> cooccs[:3]
[('c', 'k'), ('a', 'a'), ('t', 't')]
>>> len(cooccs)
17

The guide to preparing data covers the other options: whole sequences, n-grams, files and presence–absence matrices.

docs.title: Handle sparse data
docs.text:
Real data has many rare pairs, for which raw relative frequencies are unreliable. A scorer can smooth its probabilities, here with Laplace smoothing:

>>> smoothed = asymcat.CatScorer(cooccs, smoothing_method="laplace")
>>> [round(v, 2) for v in smoothed.mle()[("c", "k")]]
[0.5, 0.6]

The information-theoretic measures can also use bias-corrected entropy estimators; see Work with sparse data.

docs.title: Test significance
docs.text:
A score is only as good as the evidence behind it. permutation_pvalue tests any measure against independence by shuffling the data:

>>> pvalues = smoothed.permutation_pvalue("theil_u", n_permutations=499, seed=0)
>>> [round(p, 3) for p in pvalues[("c", "k")]]
[0.872, 1.0]

With five words, the data cannot tell the association of c with /k/ from chance: shuffled data score at least as high most of the time. Test significance and uncertainty covers the parametric tests, bootstrap confidence intervals and testing many pairs at once.

docs.title: Turn scores into matrices
docs.text:
To plot or analyse the scores of all pairs at once, scorer2matrices arranges a measure as two matrices, one for each direction:

>>> from asymcat.scorer import scorer2matrices
>>> xy, yx, letters, sounds = scorer2matrices(smoothed.theil_u())
>>> xy.shape, yx.shape
((9, 8), (8, 9))
>>> letters[:4], sounds[:4]
(['a', 'c', 'e', 'i'], ['a', 'e', 'i', 'k'])

xy[i, j] is the score of letters[i] predicting sounds[j], and yx[j, i] that of sounds[j] predicting letters[i]. Plot score matrices draws them as heatmaps.

docs.text:

  • Pitfalls lists the surprises to watch for.
  • The measure pages define each measure.
  • The API reference documents every function.

docs.title: How-to guides
docs.text:
Task-oriented guides, each answering one practical question. They assume you have read the Tutorial.

  • Prepare co-occurrence data: from table columns, aligned sequences, n-grams, whole sequences, files and presence–absence matrices.
  • Work with sparse data: smoothing the probabilities and correcting the entropies.
  • Test significance and uncertainty: parametric tests, permutation tests, bootstrap confidence intervals and testing many pairs.
  • Rank, scale and compare scores: ranking pairs, finding asymmetric ones, rescaling and combining measures.
  • Plot score matrices: heatmaps of both directions.
  • Summarise whole variables: one number for two whole variables, rather than one per pair.

docs.title: Rank, scale and compare scores
docs.text:
A measure returns a dictionary from pairs to \((x \to y,\ y \to x)\) tuples. This guide shows common ways to work with that dictionary: ranking pairs, finding the most asymmetric ones, and rescaling scores.

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> mle = scorer.mle()

docs.title: Rank pairs in one direction
docs.text:
Sort the pairs by the score in the direction you care about: index 0 for \(x \to y\), index 1 for \(y \to x\).

>>> by_letter = sorted(mle, key=lambda pair: mle[pair][0], reverse=True)
>>> by_letter[:3]
[('k', 'k'), ('q', 'k'), ('c', 'k')]
>>> by_sound = sorted(mle, key=lambda pair: mle[pair][1], reverse=True)
>>> by_sound[:3]
[('c', 's'), ('c', 'k'), ('k', 'k')]

Letters are the best predictors of sounds for k and q (always /k/); sounds are the best predictors of letters for /s/ (always c). Sort in ascending order for conditional entropy, where lower is stronger.

docs.title: Find the most asymmetric pairs
docs.text:
The difference between the two directions shows where prediction runs one way:

>>> asymmetry = {pair: xy - yx for pair, (xy, yx) in mle.items()}
>>> for pair in sorted(asymmetry, key=lambda p: abs(asymmetry[p]), reverse=True)[:3]:
...     print(pair, round(asymmetry[pair], 2))
('q', 'k') 0.82
('k', 'k') 0.73
('c', 's') -0.6

Positive values mean that \(x\) predicts \(y\) better than the reverse. Only directional measures give non-zero differences; see Directional association.

docs.title: Keep only observed pairs
docs.text:
Measures score every combination of values, including pairs never observed. The observation counts are in scorer.obs, where "11" is \(c(x, y)\):

>>> observed = {pair: score for pair, score in mle.items() if scorer.obs[pair]["11"] > 0}
>>> sorted(observed)
[('c', 'k'), ('c', 's'), ('k', 'k'), ('q', 'k')]

docs.title: Rescale scores
docs.text:
scale_scorer rescales both directions together, so that scores from different measures can be compared or combined. "minmax" maps them to a range (by default \([0, 1]\)), "mean" centres them on the mean and divides by the range, and "stdev" standardizes them:

>>> from asymcat.scorer import scale_scorer
>>> pmi = scorer.pmi()
>>> scaled = scale_scorer(pmi, method="minmax")
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scaled[("c", "s")]]
[1.0, 1.0]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scaled[("k", "s")]]
[0.0, 0.0]

Scaling cannot handle infinite values, such as Fisher's odds ratio for tables with an empty cell.

docs.title: Invert scores
docs.text:
invert_scorer subtracts every score from the largest one, turning a measure where lower is stronger into one where higher is stronger:

>>> from asymcat.scorer import invert_scorer
>>> inverted = invert_scorer(scorer.cond_entropy())
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in inverted[("q", "k")]]
[0.995, 0.0]

docs.title: Combine measures
docs.text:
To combine measures with different scales, rank or scale each one first. For example, the average rank of each pair under two measures, for \(x \to y\):

>>> def ranks(scores, direction=0):
...     order = sorted(scores, key=lambda pair: scores[pair][direction], reverse=True)
...     return {pair: rank for rank, pair in enumerate(order, start=1)}
>>> mle_ranks, theil_ranks = ranks(mle), ranks(scorer.theil_u())
>>> average = {pair: (mle_ranks[pair] + theil_ranks[pair]) / 2 for pair in observed}
>>> sorted(average, key=average.get)
[('k', 'k'), ('q', 'k'), ('c', 'k'), ('c', 's')]

Ties share the order in which the scorer lists the pairs; break them explicitly, for example by the count scorer.obs[pair]["11"], when the order matters.

docs.title: Plot score matrices
docs.text: A heatmap shows the scores of all pairs at once. scorer2matrices arranges a measure as two matrices, one per direction, which any plotting library can draw. The examples use matplotlib, which pip install "asymcat[viz]" installs.

docs.title: From scores to matrices
docs.text:
>>> import asymcat
>>> from asymcat.scorer import scorer2matrices
>>> words = [
...     ("cat", "kat"),
...     ("cot", "kot"),
...     ("city", "siti"),
...     ("kit", "kit"),
...     ("cent", "sent"),
...     ("cell", "sel-"),
...     ("kid", "kid"),
...     ("coin", "koin"),
... ]
>>> scorer = asymcat.CatScorer(asymcat.collect_cooccs(words, order=1))
>>> xy, yx, letters, sounds = scorer2matrices(scorer.mle())
>>> xy.shape, yx.shape
((11, 11), (11, 11))

xy[i, j] is the score of letters[i] as a predictor of sounds[j], here \(P(\text{sound} \mid \text{letter})\); yx[j, i] is the score of sounds[j] as a predictor of letters[i]. The alphabets are sorted, and the gap symbol - marks the silent second l of "cell".

docs.title: A pair of heatmaps
docs.text:
Drawing the two directions side by side, with the same colour scale, shows where prediction runs one way:

>>> import matplotlib
>>> matplotlib.use("Agg")
>>> import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
>>> fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.5), constrained_layout=True)
>>> panels = [(xy, letters, sounds, "P(sound | letter)"), (yx, sounds, letters, "P(letter | sound)")]
>>> for ax, (matrix, rows, cols, title) in zip(axes, panels):
...     image = ax.imshow(matrix, vmin=0, vmax=1, cmap="Blues")
...     _ = ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols)), cols)
...     _ = ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)), rows)
...     _ = ax.set_title(title)
>>> _ = fig.colorbar(image, ax=axes, shrink=0.8)
>>> fig.savefig("mle.png", dpi=150)

Each row of the left panel sums to 1: the letter c splits between /k/ and /s/, while most other letters map to a single sound. In the right panel, /k/ splits among c and k. The figure is produced by this code when the documentation is built.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Fix the colour scale (vmin, vmax) when comparing directions or measures, so that the same colour means the same value.
  • Use a diverging colour map (such as "RdBu", centred on 0) for signed measures such as PMI and the Tresoldi measure.
  • Mask unobserved pairs, which get conventional scores (see Pitfalls), for example with numpy.ma.masked_where on a matrix built from scorer.obs.
  • Order rows and columns by frequency or by a clustering of the scores when the alphabets are large; the matrices follow the order of the alphabet lists, so reorder both together.

docs.title: Prepare co-occurrence data
docs.text: CatScorer takes a list of co-occurrences: pairs \((x, y)\) of values observed together. This guide shows how to build that list from the usual shapes of data.

docs.title: Two columns of a table
docs.text:
When each observation has a value for both variables, as two columns of a table, pair them with zip:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> odour = ["almond", "anise", "none", "pungent", "none", "foul"]
>>> edible = ["yes", "yes", "yes", "no", "no", "no"]
>>> pairs = list(zip(odour, edible))
>>> pairs[:2]
[('almond', 'yes'), ('anise', 'yes')]
>>> CatScorer(pairs).mle()[("pungent", "no")]
(1.0, 0.3333333333333333)

With pandas, list(zip(df["odour"], df["class"])) does the same.

docs.title: Aligned sequences
docs.text:
For pairs of sequences whose elements correspond position by position, such as a spelling and its pronunciation aligned symbol by symbol, use collect_cooccs with order=1. Sequences can be strings or lists:

>>> import asymcat
>>> aligned = [("cat", "kat"), (["c", "e", "n", "t"], ["s", "e", "n", "t"])]
>>> asymcat.collect_cooccs(aligned, order=1)
[('c', 'k'), ('a', 'a'), ('t', 't'), ('c', 's'), ('e', 'e'), ('n', 'n'), ('t', 't')]

The two sequences of a pair must have the same length. Alignment itself, such as inserting gaps where a letter is silent, is up to you; a gap symbol such as "-" is a value like any other.

docs.title: Contexts: n-grams
docs.text:
With a larger order, collect_cooccs pairs every element of an n-gram of one sequence with every element of the corresponding n-gram of the other, so that each symbol also co-occurs with its neighbours:

>>> asymcat.collect_cooccs([("cat", "kat")], order=2)
[('c', 'k'), ('c', 'k'), ('c', 'a'), ('a', 'k'), ('a', 'a'), ('a', 'a'), ('a', 't'), ('t', 'a'), ('t', 't'), ('t', 't')]

The sequences are padded with pad="#" (by default) so that the first and last elements occur in as many n-grams as the others, and pairs involving the pad symbol are dropped. The pad symbol must not occur in the data. collect_ngrams returns the n-grams themselves:

>>> list(asymcat.collect_ngrams("cat", 2, "#"))
[('#', 'c'), ('c', 'a'), ('a', 't'), ('t', '#')]

docs.title: Whole sequences
docs.text:
Without order, collect_cooccs pairs every element of one sequence with every element of the other, whatever their positions. This suits pairs of unordered collections, such as the tags of a document and the words of its title:

>>> asymcat.collect_cooccs([(["red", "round"], ["apple"]), (["red"], ["cherry", "apple"])])
[('red', 'apple'), ('round', 'apple'), ('red', 'cherry'), ('red', 'apple')]

A pair of sequences of lengths \(m\) and \(k\) contributes \(m \times k\) co-occurrences, so long sequences weigh more; see Pitfalls.

docs.title: Sequences from a file
docs.text:
read_sequences reads a tab-separated file with one pair of sequences per row and elements separated by spaces, skipping the header row:

>>> from pathlib import Path
>>> _ = Path("spelling.tsv").write_text(
...     "Orthography\tSegments\nc a t\tk a t\nc e n t\ts e n t\n",
...     encoding="utf-8",
... )
>>> data = asymcat.read_sequences("spelling.tsv")
>>> data
[[['c', 'a', 't'], ['k', 'a', 't']], [['c', 'e', 'n', 't'], ['s', 'e', 'n', 't']]]
>>> len(asymcat.collect_cooccs(data, order=1))
7

With cols=["Orthography", "Segments"], it reads the named columns of a file with more than two. col_delim and elem_delim change the separators.

docs.title: Presence–absence matrices
docs.text:
In a presence–absence matrix, each row is a site and each column records whether a taxon (or feature) was observed there. read_pa_matrix turns it into co-occurrences: one pair for every two taxa present at the same site. The file needs an ID column for the sites:

>>> _ = Path("islands.tsv").write_text(
...     "ID\tfinch\tgecko\tiguana\nnorth\t1\t1\t0\nsouth\t1\t1\t1\nwest\t0\t1\t1\n",
...     encoding="utf-8",
... )
>>> asymcat.read_pa_matrix("islands.tsv")
[('finch', 'gecko'), ('finch', 'gecko'), ('finch', 'iguana'), ('gecko', 'iguana'), ('gecko', 'iguana')]

Each pair is ordered alphabetically, so a taxon appears as \(x\) or \(y\) depending on its name; the Jaccard index and the other symmetric measures are the natural choice for such data.

docs.title: Test significance and uncertainty
docs.text:
A score computed from a few co-occurrences can be large by chance. ASymCat offers three kinds of tools to judge the evidence: the p-values of the classical tests, permutation tests for any measure, and bootstrap confidence intervals.

The examples use the example data repeated four times, so that there is some evidence to test:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs * 4)

docs.title: Parametric tests
docs.text:
Three measures have a classical test of independence for the 2×2 table of each pair:

>>> round(scorer.chi2_pvalue()[("c", "s")][0], 4)
0.0028
>>> round(scorer.log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue()[("c", "s")][0], 4)
0.0001
>>> round(scorer.fisher_pvalue()[("c", "s")][0], 4)
0.0005

Fisher's exact test is the safest with small counts; the chi-square and G² tests rely on a large-sample approximation. All three are symmetric: both tuple entries hold the same p-value.

docs.title: Permutation tests for any measure
docs.text:
permutation_pvalue tests any measure, directional ones included, against the hypothesis that the two variables are independent. It shuffles which \(y\) goes with which \(x\), which keeps both sets of frequencies and destroys the association, recomputes the measure, and reports how often the shuffled score is at least as extreme as the observed one:

>>> pvalues = scorer.permutation_pvalue("theil_u", n_permutations=999, seed=0)
>>> [round(p, 3) for p in pvalues[("c", "k")]]
[0.003, 0.003]

With four times the data, the association of c with /k/ is now significant in both directions. The result has one p-value per direction. alternative selects the tail: "greater" (the default) when larger scores mean stronger association, "less" for conditional entropy, and "two-sided" for either. The smallest possible p-value is \(1/(\texttt{n_permutations} + 1)\), so use more permutations to resolve small p-values. Use seed to make the result reproducible.

docs.title: Confidence intervals
docs.text:
bootstrap_ci gives a percentile confidence interval for each score, by recomputing the measure on resamples of the co-occurrences drawn with replacement:

>>> intervals = scorer.bootstrap_ci("mle", n_bootstrap=999, confidence_level=0.95, seed=0)
>>> (low_xy, high_xy), (low_yx, high_yx) = intervals[("c", "k")]
>>> round(low_xy, 2), round(high_xy, 2)
(0.45, 0.75)

With 60 co-occurrences, \(P(k \mid c) = 0.6\) could plausibly lie anywhere between 0.45 and 0.75. The point estimate is the measure itself (scorer.mle()). Wide intervals mark scores that the data does not pin down, which is common for rare symbols even after smoothing.

Both resampling methods accept the measures in CatScorer.RESAMPLABLE_MEASURES, computed with their default parameters, and use the scorer's smoothing and entropy settings.

docs.title: Many pairs, many tests
docs.text:
A scorer tests every pair, so some p-values will be small by chance. Control the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) across the pairs with SciPy:

>>> from scipy.stats import false_discovery_control
>>> pvalues = scorer.fisher_pvalue()
>>> pairs_tested = sorted(pvalues)
>>> adjusted = false_discovery_control([pvalues[pair][0] for pair in pairs_tested])
>>> [pair for pair, p in zip(pairs_tested, adjusted) if p < 0.05]
[('c', 'k'), ('c', 's'), ('k', 'k'), ('k', 's')]

The pairs of q are not significant after the correction: two observations of q, even repeated four times, are little evidence.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The tests treat co-occurrences as independent observations. Co-occurrences collected from sequences are not, so p-values are somewhat too small and intervals too narrow when sequences are long.
  • A significant association can be an avoidance; check the sign of PMI or the odds ratio.
  • Significance is not strength: with enough data, a negligible association is significant. Report a measure of strength with every p-value.

docs.title: Work with sparse data
docs.text:
Categorical data is usually sparse: a few pairs are frequent and most are rare or unobserved. Raw relative frequencies are unreliable for the rare pairs, and the plug-in entropy is biased on small samples. A CatScorer has two options for this, one for probabilities and one for entropies.

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4

docs.title: Smooth the probabilities
docs.text:
smoothing_method controls the probabilities behind mle, tresoldi and pmi_smoothed. The estimates come from FreqProb:

smoothing_method Estimate of \(P(y \mid x)\) "mle" (default) \(c(x, y) / c(x)\) "laplace" \(\big(c(x, y) + 1\big) / \big(c(x) + 2\big)\) "lidstone" \(\big(c(x, y) + \gamma\big) / \big(c(x) + 2\gamma\big)\), \(\gamma\) = smoothing_alpha 
>>> for method in ("mle", "laplace", "lidstone"):
...     mle = CatScorer(pairs, smoothing_method=method, smoothing_alpha=0.5).mle()
...     print(method, [round(p, 3) for p in mle[("q", "k")]])
mle [1.0, 0.182]
laplace [0.75, 0.231]
lidstone [0.833, 0.208]

With only two observations of q, Laplace smoothing pulls \(P(k \mid q)\) from 1 to 0.75; Lidstone with \(\gamma = 0.5\) pulls it less. Smoothing matters most for rare symbols and leaves frequent ones nearly unchanged.

pmi_smoothed smooths the joint distribution of the pairs with the same setting, and derives the marginal probabilities from it:

>>> laplace = CatScorer(pairs, smoothing_method="laplace")
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in laplace.pmi_smoothed()[("c", "s")]]
[0.223, 0.223]

docs.title: Correct the entropies
docs.text:
entropy_estimator controls the entropies behind theil_u, cond_entropy and mutual information. The plug-in estimate underestimates entropy on small samples, because it ignores values that were possible but not observed. FreqProb provides two corrections:

  • "chao_shen" (Chao & Shen, 2003) corrects for unseen values using the number of values seen once.
  • "nsb" (Nemenman, Shafee & Bialek, 2002) is a Bayesian estimator that takes the number of possible values into account; ASymCat gives it the alphabet sizes of the data.
>>> for estimator in ("plugin", "chao_shen", "nsb"):
...     theil_u = CatScorer(pairs, entropy_estimator=estimator).theil_u()
...     print(estimator, [round(u, 3) for u in theil_u[("c", "k")]])
plugin [0.226, 0.152]
chao_shen [0.225, 0.144]
nsb [0.301, 0.197]

The corrected estimates are not confined to \([0, 1]\); a slightly negative value on a small subset means no detectable association. The NSB estimator is slower than the other two, which matters with the resampling tools.

docs.title: Which to use
docs.text:
• With plenty of data for every symbol, the defaults are fine.
  • Use "laplace" or "lidstone" when conditional probabilities of rare symbols matter, and always with pmi_smoothed.
  • Use "chao_shen" or "nsb" when the information-theoretic measures are computed on small pair subsets.
  • Whatever the setting, check rare pairs with bootstrap_ci: smoothing makes estimates more stable, not more certain.

docs.title: Summarise whole variables
docs.text:
CatScorer scores pairs of values. To summarise the association between two whole variables (all letters against all sounds) with a single number, use the functions in asymcat.correlation. They take two aligned series of the same length, one value per observation:

>>> from asymcat import correlation
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> letters = [x for x, _ in pairs]
>>> sounds = [y for _, y in pairs]

docs.title: Theil's U
docs.text:
correlation.theil_u(series_x, series_y) is \(U(X \mid Y)\): the share of the uncertainty about the first series that knowing the second removes.

>>> round(correlation.theil_u(sounds, letters), 3)  # sounds predicted from letters
0.226
>>> round(correlation.theil_u(letters, sounds), 3)  # letters predicted from sounds
0.152

Knowing the letter removes 23% of the uncertainty about the sound; knowing the sound removes 15% of the uncertainty about the letter. On this dataset, the pair subset of c and /k/ is the whole dataset, so CatScorer.theil_u gives the same numbers for that pair.

docs.title: Conditional entropy
docs.text:
correlation.conditional_entropy(series_x, series_y) is \(H(X \mid Y)\), in nats:

>>> round(correlation.conditional_entropy(sounds, letters), 3)
0.449
>>> round(correlation.conditional_entropy(letters, sounds), 3)
0.73

Both functions accept estimator="chao_shen" or "nsb" for bias-corrected entropies (see Work with sparse data).

docs.title: Cramér's V
docs.text:
correlation.cramers_v(series_x, series_y) is the bias-corrected Cramér's V of the full contingency table of the two series. It is symmetric:

>>> round(correlation.cramers_v(letters, sounds), 3)
0.205

Over the whole 3×2 table, the association is weak. For each pair's own 2×2 table, the bias correction finds no association beyond chance on 15 observations; see Chi-square and Cramér's V.

docs.title: Measures
docs.text:
Every measure is a method of CatScorer and returns, for each pair \((x, y)\), a tuple \((x \to y,\ y \to x)\) (see Notation). Each page below gives the definition as ASymCat computes it, a worked example on the same example data, its properties and caveats, the API entry and the references.

Measure Method Direction Range Computed on Conditional probability mle directional \([0, 1]\) counts Pointwise mutual information pmi, pmi_smoothed symmetric \((-\infty, \infty)\); NPMI \([-1, 1]\) counts Theil's U theil_u directional \([0, 1]\) pair subset Conditional entropy cond_entropy directional \([0, \infty)\), lower is stronger pair subset Mutual information mutual_information, normalized_mutual_information symmetric \([0, \infty)\); NMI \([0, 1]\) pair subset Chi-square and Cramér's V chi2, chi2_pvalue, cramers_v symmetric \([0, \infty)\); V \([0, 1]\) 2×2 table Fisher's exact test fisher, fisher_pvalue symmetric odds ratio \([0, \infty]\) 2×2 table Log-likelihood ratio log_likelihood_ratio, log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue symmetric \([0, \infty)\) 2×2 table Goodman–Kruskal λ goodman_kruskal_lambda directional \([0, 1]\) pair subset Jaccard index jaccard_index symmetric \([0, 1]\) counts The Tresoldi measure tresoldi directional \((-\infty, \infty)\) counts

"Computed on" says which view of the pair a measure uses: the counts \(c(x, y)\), \(c(x)\) and \(c(y)\) directly; the 2×2 contingency table over all co-occurrences; or the pair subset of co-occurrences that contain \(x\) or \(y\).

To decide which measure answers your question, see Choosing a measure. For p-values and confidence intervals for any of them, see Test significance and uncertainty.

docs.title: Chi-square and Cramér's V
docs.text:
CatScorer.chi2(), CatScorer.chi2_pvalue(), CatScorer.cramers_v() · symmetric · statistical

Pearson's chi-square statistic (Pearson, 1900) measures how far the 2×2 contingency table of a pair departs from what independence predicts, and its p-value tests whether the departure could be due to chance. Cramér's V (Cramér, 1946) rescales the statistic to \([0, 1]\), so that it reports the strength of the association rather than the amount of evidence for it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(O_{ij}\) the observed counts of the 2×2 table and \(E_{ij} = (\text{row total}_i \times \text{column total}_j) / n\) the counts expected under independence,

\[ \chi^2 = \sum_{i, j} \frac{\big(|O_{ij} - E_{ij}| - \tfrac{1}{2}\big)^2}{E_{ij}}. \]

The \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) is Yates' (1934) continuity correction, which SciPy's chi2_contingency applies to 2×2 tables and ASymCat keeps. chi2_pvalue returns the p-value of the test, from the \(\chi^2\) distribution with one degree of freedom.

cramers_v uses the bias-corrected form of Bergsma (2013), which subtracts the value expected under independence before taking the root. With \(\varphi^2 = \chi^2 / n\) and an \(r \times k\) table:

\[ V = \sqrt{\frac{\tilde\varphi^2}{\min(\tilde k - 1, \tilde r - 1)}},\quad \tilde\varphi^2 = \max\!\Big(0,\ \varphi^2 - \frac{(k-1)(r-1)}{n-1}\Big),\quad \tilde r = r - \frac{(r-1)^2}{n-1},\quad \tilde k = k - \frac{(k-1)^2}{n-1}. \]

All three are symmetric, so both tuple entries are equal.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
The example data has only 15 co-occurrences. Repeating it ten times keeps the same proportions with ten times the evidence:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> small, large = CatScorer(pairs), CatScorer(pairs * 10)
>>> round(small.chi2()[("c", "k")][0], 3), round(large.chi2()[("c", "k")][0], 3)
(1.065, 25.266)
>>> round(small.chi2_pvalue()[("c", "k")][0], 3), large.chi2_pvalue()[("c", "k")][0] < 0.001
(0.302, True)
>>> round(small.cramers_v()[("c", "k")][0], 3), round(large.cramers_v()[("c", "k")][0], 3)
(0.0, 0.404)

The statistic grows with the sample, and the same association becomes significant. Cramér's V does not grow with \(n\) in the same way, but the bias correction sets it to 0 when, as in the small sample, the association is no larger than independence would produce by chance.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Symmetric. Both entries are equal, and with only two values of \(y\), the tables of \((x, y_1)\) and \((x, y_2)\) are mirror images and get the same score.
  • Unsigned. The statistic is the same for attraction and avoidance; check the sign of PMI for the direction of the departure.
  • Small expected counts. The \(\chi^2\) approximation is unreliable when expected counts are small (a common rule of thumb is below 5). Yates' correction makes the test conservative; Fisher's exact test avoids the approximation.
  • Many tests. Scoring every pair runs one test per pair; see Test significance.

docs.title: Conditional entropy
docs.text:
CatScorer.cond_entropy() · directional · range \([0, \infty)\) nats · information-theoretic

The conditional entropy \(H(Y \mid X)\) is the uncertainty about \(Y\) that remains once \(X\) is known. Unlike most measures, lower means stronger: 0 means that \(X\) determines \(Y\). It is the unnormalized quantity behind Theil's U.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[ H(Y \mid X) = -\sum_{x, y} P(x, y) \ln P(y \mid x) = H(X, Y) - H(X) \]

As for Theil's U, the variables are the first and second elements of the pair subset \(S(x, y)\):

\[ \texttt{cond_entropy}(x, y) = \big(H(Y_S \mid X_S),\ H(X_S \mid Y_S)\big) \]

The entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator; with "chao_shen" or "nsb", the two terms of \(H(X, Y) - H(X)\) are corrected separately.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> cond_entropy = CatScorer(pairs).cond_entropy()
>>> [round(h, 3) for h in cond_entropy[("c", "k")]]
[0.449, 0.73]
>>> [round(h, 3) for h in cond_entropy[("q", "k")]]
[0.0, 0.995]

Once the letter is known, 0.449 nats of uncertainty about the sound remain across the whole dataset (the subset of c and /k/). In the subset of q and /k/, the sound is always /k/, so nothing remains to predict (\(0\)), while the letter keeps almost all its uncertainty (0.995 nats, close to \(\ln 3 \approx 1.10\) for three letters).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Directional, and lower is stronger: rank pairs in ascending order, and use alternative="less" with permutation_pvalue.
  • Not normalized. Its scale depends on the number of values in the subset; Theil's U divides it out, which makes pairs comparable.
  • Unsigned, as for the other measures on the pair subset: see Pitfalls.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The whole-variable version is asymcat.correlation.conditional_entropy.

cond_entropy() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

For every pair (x, y) this computes the conditional entropy in both directions over the subset of co-occurrences where pair[0] == x or pair[1] == y, matching conditional_entropy(Y, X) and conditional_entropy(X, Y) on that subset. The entropies come from the same computation as theil_u (see _subset_entropy_components) and follow the scorer's entropy_estimator.

docs.title: Fisher's exact test
docs.text:
CatScorer.fisher(), CatScorer.fisher_pvalue() · symmetric · statistical

Fisher's exact test (Fisher, 1922) tests the independence of the two rows of a 2×2 table without the large-sample approximation of chi-square. It is the test to use when counts are small. fisher returns the sample odds ratio of the table and fisher_pvalue the two-sided p-value of the test, both from SciPy's fisher_exact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For the table

\(y\) not \(y\) \(x\) \(a\) \(b\) not \(x\) \(c\) \(d\)

the odds ratio is

\[ \mathrm{OR} = \frac{a\,d}{b\,c}: \]

the odds of \(y\) when \(x\) is present, divided by the odds of \(y\) when it is not. \(\mathrm{OR} > 1\) means attraction and \(\mathrm{OR} < 1\) avoidance. The p-value is the probability, with the margins of the table fixed, of a table at least as unlikely as the one observed. Both are symmetric, so both tuple entries are equal.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> scorer.fisher()[("c", "s")], scorer.fisher()[("c", "k")]
((inf, inf), (0.0, 0.0))
>>> [round(p, 3) for p in scorer.fisher_pvalue()[("c", "s")]]
[0.231, 0.231]

Every /s/ is spelled c, so the table of c and /s/ has \(c = 0\) and an infinite odds ratio; the table of c and /k/ has \(d = 0\) and an odds ratio of 0. Even so, with 15 observations the association is not significant (\(p = 0.23\)).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Exact. The p-value does not rely on large counts, which makes it the safest of the statistical tests for sparse data.
  • Signed through the odds ratio, around 1 rather than 0. Its logarithm is symmetric around 0.
  • Infinite and zero odds ratios. Any empty cell gives \(\mathrm{OR} = 0\) or \(\infty\), which is common with categorical data. Such values break scale_scorer; rank by the p-value or use the smoothed conditional probability instead.
  • Many tests. See Test significance.

It is the unconditional maximum-likelihood estimate; R's fisher.test reports the conditional one, which differs slightly. A table with an empty cell gives an odds ratio of 0 or inf. Both tuple entries hold the same value; the p-values are given by fisher_pvalue.

docs.title: Goodman–Kruskal λ
docs.text:
CatScorer.goodman_kruskal_lambda() · directional · range \([0, 1]\) · statistical

Goodman and Kruskal's λ (Goodman & Kruskal, 1954) is the proportional reduction in prediction errors: if you must guess \(Y\), how many fewer mistakes do you make by knowing \(X\)? Without \(X\), the best guess is always the most frequent \(y\); with it, the most frequent \(y\) for each \(x\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(n(x, y)\) the counts of a table, \(n(y)\) its column totals and \(N\) its total,

\[ \lambda(Y \mid X) = \frac{\sum_x \max_y n(x, y) - \max_y n(y)}{N - \max_y n(y)}, \]

with \(\lambda = 1\) by convention when the denominator is 0 (when \(Y\) takes a single value, so that there are no errors to reduce), as for Theil's U. In ASymCat, the table is the pair subset \(S(x, y)\):

\[ \texttt{goodman_kruskal_lambda}(x, y) = \big(\lambda(Y_S \mid X_S),\ \lambda(X_S \mid Y_S)\big) \]

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> gk_lambda = CatScorer(pairs).goodman_kruskal_lambda()
>>> gk_lambda[("c", "k")]
(0.0, 0.0)
>>> gk_lambda[("k", "s")]
(1.0, 1.0)

For c and /k/, the subset is the whole dataset. Without the letter, the best guess for the sound is /k/, right 11 times in 15. Knowing the letter does not change any guess, since /k/ is also the most frequent sound for each letter, so λ is 0, although Theil's U finds that the letter carries information about the sound (0.23). In the subset of k and /s/, each variable determines the other.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Directional. \(\lambda(Y \mid X) \neq \lambda(X \mid Y)\) in general.
  • Zero despite association. λ only registers associations that change the modal guess. When one value dominates every row, λ is 0 whatever the association; Theil's U is more sensitive.
  • A convention on degenerate subsets. When the predicted variable takes a single value in the subset, λ is 1, as is Theil's U: for ("q", "k"), both give 1 and 0.
  • Unsigned, as for the other measures on the pair subset: see Pitfalls.

Computes λ(Y|X) and λ(X|Y) for each symbol pair, measuring the proportional reduction in error when predicting one variable from another. Like theil_u, it is computed on the subset of co-occurrences where pair[0] == x or pair[1] == y; when the predicted variable takes a single value in that subset, the score is 1.0, as for theil_u.

docs.title: Jaccard index
docs.text:
CatScorer.jaccard_index() · symmetric · range \([0, 1]\) · set-based

The Jaccard index (Jaccard, 1912) is the overlap of two sets divided by their union. Here, the sets are the co-occurrences that contain \(x\) and those that contain \(y\): the index is the share of the co-occurrences involving either symbol that involve both.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[ J(x, y) = \frac{|A_x \cap A_y|}{|A_x \cup A_y|} = \frac{c(x, y)}{c(x) + c(y) - c(x, y)} \]

where \(A_x\) is the set of co-occurrences whose first element is \(x\), and \(A_y\) the set whose second element is \(y\). It is 0 when \(x\) and \(y\) never co-occur, and 1 when they only ever occur together. The index is symmetric, so both tuple entries are equal.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> jaccard = CatScorer(pairs).jaccard_index()
>>> jaccard[("c", "k")], jaccard[("c", "s")]
((0.4, 0.4), (0.4, 0.4))
>>> [round(j, 3) for j in jaccard[("q", "k")]]
[0.182, 0.182]

c and /k/ share 6 of the \(10 + 11 - 6 = 15\) co-occurrences that involve either; c and /s/ share 4 of 10.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Symmetric and bounded, with a simple reading as overlap.
  • Not corrected for chance. Frequent symbols overlap more by chance, and the index does not distinguish attraction from mere frequency. Use PMI for that.
  • Natural for presence–absence data, where co-occurrences are joint presences at a site (see Prepare co-occurrence data).
  • Related to the conditional probabilities. \(1/J = 1/P(y \mid x) + 1/P(x \mid y) - 1\), so \(J\) is high only when both are high.

docs.title: Log-likelihood ratio (G²)
docs.text:
CatScorer.log_likelihood_ratio(), CatScorer.log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue() · symmetric · statistical

The log-likelihood ratio statistic \(G^2\) compares the likelihood of the 2×2 table under independence with its likelihood without that constraint. Dunning (1993) introduced it to computational linguistics as an alternative to chi-square for rare events, and it is widely used for collocation extraction.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
With \(O_{ij}\) the observed and \(E_{ij}\) the expected counts of the table, as for chi-square,

\[ G^2 = 2 \sum_{i, j} O_{ij} \ln \frac{O_{ij}}{E_{ij}}, \]

where empty cells contribute 0. ASymCat applies no continuity correction. log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue returns the p-value from the \(\chi^2\) distribution with one degree of freedom, which \(G^2\) follows asymptotically under independence. Both are symmetric, so both tuple entries are equal.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> round(scorer.log_likelihood_ratio()[("c", "k")][0], 3)
3.937
>>> round(scorer.log_likelihood_ratio_pvalue()[("c", "k")][0], 3)
0.047

On the same table, the Yates-corrected chi-square gives \(p = 0.30\) and Fisher's exact test \(p = 0.23\). With so few observations, the asymptotic tests disagree, and the exact test is the one to trust.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Additive. \(G^2\) decomposes over nested tables, which makes it convenient for model comparison.
  • Asymptotically equivalent to chi-square, and neither is reliable when expected counts are small: without a continuity correction, \(G^2\) tends to be anti-conservative there, as above. Prefer Fisher's exact test for sparse tables.
  • Unsigned. Check the sign of PMI or the odds ratio for the direction of the departure.

docs.title: Conditional probability (mle)
docs.text:
CatScorer.mle() · directional · range \([0, 1]\) · probabilistic

The conditional probability is the most direct directional measure: how often \(y\) occurs when \(x\) does, and how often \(x\) occurs when \(y\) does. It is the natural first measure to look at, and the one the others are best compared with.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[ \texttt{mle}(x, y) = \big(P(y \mid x),\ P(x \mid y)\big) = \left(\frac{c(x, y)}{c(x)},\ \frac{c(x, y)}{c(y)}\right) \]

The name refers to the maximum-likelihood estimate, which is what these relative frequencies are. With a smoothing method, the estimates are instead computed by FreqProb on the two-outcome distribution "\(y\) or not \(y\)" among the co-occurrences of \(x\) (and likewise in the other direction):

smoothing_method \(P(y \mid x)\) "mle" (default) \(c(x, y) / c(x)\) "laplace" \(\big(c(x, y) + 1\big) / \big(c(x) + 2\big)\) "lidstone" \(\big(c(x, y) + \gamma\big) / \big(c(x) + 2\gamma\big)\), with \(\gamma\) = smoothing_alpha

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> mle = CatScorer(pairs).mle()
>>> mle[("q", "k")]
(1.0, 0.18181818181818182)
>>> [round(p, 3) for p in mle[("c", "k")]]
[0.6, 0.545]
>>> mle[("q", "s")]
(0.0, 0.0)

q is always /k/, but only 2 of the 11 /k/ are spelled q. c is /k/ six times in ten, and 6 of the 11 /k/ are c. The pair q–/s/ is never observed, so both probabilities are 0.

Smoothing moves mass towards the unobserved outcome, most visibly where counts are small:

>>> laplace = CatScorer(pairs, smoothing_method="laplace").mle()
>>> [round(p, 3) for p in laplace[("q", "k")]]
[0.75, 0.231]
>>> [round(p, 3) for p in laplace[("q", "s")]]
[0.25, 0.167]

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Directional. \(P(y \mid x) \neq P(x \mid y)\) unless \(c(x) = c(y)\).
  • Bounded and interpretable. Each score is a probability.
  • Not corrected for chance. A frequent \(y\) has a high \(P(y \mid x)\) for most \(x\), whether or not \(x\) and \(y\) are associated. Compare with the base rate \(P(y)\), or use PMI or Theil's U, which account for it.
  • Unstable for rare symbols. With \(c(x) = 2\), the only possible values are 0, 0.5 and 1. Smoothing, or the resampling tools, help judge how much to trust them.

docs.title: mle
docs.text:
mle() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return an MLE scorer of conditional probabilities, computing it if necessary.

For every pair (x, y) the tuple is (P(y|x), P(x|y)): how well x predicts y, then how well y predicts x. This is the same X→Y, Y→X order as theil_u, cond_entropy and goodman_kruskal_lambda. With smoothing_method set to "laplace" or "lidstone", the probabilities are smoothed with freqprob.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (P(y|x), P(x|y)) tuples.
