docs.title: Mutual information
docs.text:
CatScorer.mutual_information(), CatScorer.normalized_mutual_information() · symmetric · range \([0, \infty)\) nats, or \([0, 1]\) normalized · information-theoretic

Mutual information (MI) is the amount of information two variables share: how much knowing one reduces the uncertainty about the other, on average. It is zero when they are independent. It is the numerator of Theil's U, before division by the entropy of one variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[ I(X; Y) = \sum_{x, y} P(x, y) \ln \frac{P(x, y)}{P(x)\,P(y)} = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X) = H(X) - H(X \mid Y) \]

The normalized mutual information divides by the joint entropy, which bounds it to \([0, 1]\); it is the complement of Rajski's (1961) distance:

\[ \mathrm{NMI}(X; Y) = \frac{I(X; Y)}{H(X, Y)} \]

In ASymCat, both are computed on the pair subset \(S(x, y)\), and both tuple entries are equal. When the subset is a single cell (one \(x\) and one \(y\)), the joint entropy is zero and NMI is 0. The entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> [round(i, 3) for i in scorer.mutual_information()[("c", "k")]]
[0.131, 0.131]
>>> [round(i, 3) for i in scorer.normalized_mutual_information()[("c", "k")]]
[0.1, 0.1]
>>> [round(i, 3) for i in scorer.normalized_mutual_information()[("k", "s")]]
[1.0, 1.0]

In the subset of k and /s/ (k–/k/ and c–/s/), each variable determines the other, so NMI is 1 even though k and /s/ never co-occur.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Symmetric. For the direction, divide by one entropy instead of the joint one: that is Theil's U.
  • Unsigned. Avoidance shares as much information as attraction; see Pitfalls. For a signed, per-pair quantity, use PMI, whose average over the cells of a table is the mutual information.
  • Biased upwards on small samples with the plug-in estimator. The bias-corrected estimators reduce this, and can return slightly negative values.

docs.title: Pointwise mutual information
docs.text:
CatScorer.pmi(), CatScorer.pmi(normalized=True), CatScorer.pmi_smoothed() · symmetric · signed · information-theoretic

Pointwise mutual information (PMI) compares how often \(x\) and \(y\) co-occur with how often they would if they were independent. It is positive when the pair is more frequent than chance, negative when it is less frequent, and zero at independence. It is widely used for collocations and word association (Church & Hanks, 1990).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
\[ \mathrm{PMI}(x, y) = \ln \frac{P(x, y)}{P(x)\,P(y)} = \ln \frac{P(y \mid x)}{P(y)} = \ln \frac{P(x \mid y)}{P(x)} \]

The normalized PMI (Bouma, 2009) divides by \(-\ln P(x, y)\), which bounds it to \([-1, 1]\): 1 when \(x\) and \(y\) only ever occur together, 0 at independence.

\[ \mathrm{NPMI}(x, y) = \frac{\mathrm{PMI}(x, y)}{-\ln P(x, y)} \]

PMI is symmetric, so both tuple entries are equal. In ASymCat:

  • pmi() uses relative frequencies. A pair never observed together would have \(\mathrm{PMI} = -\infty\); it gets the floor \(P(x, y) = (1/n)^2\) instead, which gives a large negative value.
  • pmi(normalized=True) returns NPMI, with the same floor.
  • pmi_smoothed() smooths the joint distribution \(P(x, y)\) over all pairs of observed symbols with the scorer's smoothing_method, estimated by FreqProb, and takes \(P(x)\) and \(P(y)\) as its sums. It is meant for use with "laplace" or "lidstone"; see the properties below.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> pmi = scorer.pmi()
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in pmi[("c", "s")]]
[0.405, 0.405]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in pmi[("c", "k")]]
[-0.201, -0.201]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in pmi[("q", "s")]]  # never observed
[-2.079, -2.079]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.pmi(normalized=True)[("c", "s")]]
[0.307, 0.307]

c occurs with /s/ more often than independence predicts (\(\mathrm{PMI} > 0\)), and with /k/ slightly less often: most /k/ come from c, but c is frequent, so \(P(k \mid c) = 0.6\) is below the base rate \(P(k) = 11/15 \approx 0.73\).

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Symmetric. Both tuple entries are always equal. For a directional version, see the Tresoldi measure, which tempers the PMI with the conditional probability.
  • Signed. Unlike the information-theoretic measures on the pair subset, PMI separates attraction (positive) from repulsion (negative).
  • Biased towards rare pairs. A pair seen once, made of two rare symbols, can have a higher PMI than a frequent, reliable pair. NPMI reduces this effect; testing with permutation_pvalue helps decide which scores to trust.
  • Unobserved pairs depend on the floor. Their score is determined by \((1/n)^2\) and the marginals, not by evidence, so they rank below every observed pair but are not comparable across datasets of different sizes.
  • pmi_smoothed needs a smoothing method. With the default smoothing_method="mle", unobserved pairs get a near-zero probability from FreqProb and a very large negative score. With "laplace" or "lidstone", every pair receives the same pseudo-count, so unobserved pairs score below independence but by a finite amount.

docs.title: Theil's U
docs.text:
CatScorer.theil_u() · directional · range \([0, 1]\) · information-theoretic

Theil's U, or the uncertainty coefficient (Theil, 1970), is the share of the uncertainty about one variable that knowing the other removes. 0 means that knowing \(x\) says nothing about \(y\); 1 means that it determines \(y\) completely. It is the information-theoretic counterpart of the conditional probability, and corrects for the base rate.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For two variables \(X\) and \(Y\),

\[ U(Y \mid X) = \frac{H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)}{H(Y)} = \frac{I(X; Y)}{H(Y)}, \]

with \(U(Y \mid X) = 1\) by convention when \(H(Y) = 0\). In ASymCat, the variables are the first and second elements of the pair subset \(S(x, y)\), the co-occurrences whose first element is \(x\) or whose second element is \(y\):

\[ \texttt{theil_u}(x, y) = \big(U(Y_S \mid X_S),\ U(X_S \mid Y_S)\big) \]

The entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator: the plug-in (maximum-likelihood) estimate by default, or the bias-corrected "chao_shen" and "nsb" estimators from FreqProb (see Work with sparse data).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the example data:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("q", "k")] * 2 + [("c", "k")] * 6 + [("k", "k")] * 3 + [("c", "s")] * 4
>>> theil_u = CatScorer(pairs).theil_u()
>>> [round(u, 3) for u in theil_u[("c", "k")]]
[0.226, 0.152]
>>> [round(u, 3) for u in theil_u[("q", "k")]]
[1.0, 0.0]
>>> theil_u[("k", "s")]
(1.0, 1.0)
  • c and /k/: the subset is the whole dataset. Knowing the letter removes 23% of the uncertainty about the sound, and knowing the sound removes 15% of the uncertainty about the letter.
  • q and /k/: the subset is the column of /k/, where the sound is always /k/. Its entropy is zero, so \(U(Y_S \mid X_S) = 1\) by convention, and knowing the sound says nothing about which of c, k or q spelled it.
  • k and /s/: the subset holds k–/k/ and c–/s/. Each letter determines the sound and each sound the letter, so both scores are 1, although k and /s/ never occur together. Theil's U measures predictability, not attraction: see Pitfalls.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Directional. \(U(Y \mid X) \neq U(X \mid Y)\) in general; both share the numerator \(I(X; Y)\) and differ in the entropy they normalize by.
  • Corrected for the base rate. A frequent \(y\) does not by itself raise the score, unlike \(P(y \mid x)\).
  • Unsigned. Avoidance is as predictive as attraction.
  • A convention on degenerate subsets. When one variable takes a single value in the subset, its score is 1 (no uncertainty left to remove), as for Goodman–Kruskal λ.
  • Bias-corrected estimates leave \([0, 1]\). With "chao_shen" or "nsb", a slightly negative score on a small subset means no detectable association. The plug-in estimate can also print as -0.0.

docs.title: API
docs.text: The whole-variable version, for two aligned series rather than a pair of symbols, is asymcat.correlation.theil_u.

docs.title: theil_u
docs.text:
theil_u() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Theil's U uncertainty scorer.

For every pair (x, y) this computes Theil's U in both directions over the subset of co-occurrences where pair[0] == x or pair[1] == y, matching compute_theil_u(Y, X) and compute_theil_u(X, Y) on that subset. The underlying entropies are computed with a vectorized formulation (see _subset_entropy_components) that evaluates all pairs at once rather than re-filtering the co-occurrence list for each pair.

Entropies follow the scorer's entropy_estimator. Bias-corrected estimates are not confined to [0, 1]: a slightly negative value on a small subset means no detectable association.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Theil (1970); Shannon (1948); Cover & Thomas (2006). See References.

docs.title: The Tresoldi measure
docs.text:
CatScorer.tresoldi() · directional · signed · range \((-\infty, \infty)\) · specialized

The Tresoldi measure is a directional association score specific to ASymCat. It was designed for scoring alignments, such as grapheme–phoneme correspondences, where the question is how strongly one symbol is associated with another in a given direction. It combines two quantities: the pointwise mutual information (PMI) of the pair, which says how far their co-occurrence departs from independence, and the conditional probability of one symbol given the other.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a pair of symbols \((x, y)\), the score in the \(x \to y\) direction is

\[ T(x \to y) = \operatorname{sign}\big(\mathrm{PMI}(x, y)\big)\, \big|\mathrm{PMI}(x, y)\big|^{\,1 - P(y \mid x)} \]

and the \(y \to x\) score uses \(P(x \mid y)\) in the exponent instead. Here

\[ \mathrm{PMI}(x, y) = \ln \frac{P(x, y)}{P(x)\,P(y)}, \qquad P(y \mid x) = \frac{P(x, y)}{P(x)}. \]

PMI is symmetric, so the two directions differ only through the exponent: the scores coincide exactly when \(P(y \mid x) = P(x \mid y)\), that is, when \(x\) and \(y\) occur equally often.

In ASymCat:

  • PMI uses the natural logarithm and the relative frequencies of the co-occurrences, without smoothing. A pair that never co-occurs is given the floor \(P(x, y) = (1/n)^2\), with \(n\) the number of co-occurrences, which makes its PMI strongly negative.
  • The conditional probability is the one returned by CatScorer.mle(), so smoothing_method="laplace" or "lidstone" affects this term only.
  • The sign is applied outside the power, so negative PMI values never meet a fractional exponent.

docs.title: How the exponent behaves
docs.text:
The exponent \(1 - P(y \mid x)\) falls from 1 to 0 as \(x\) becomes a better predictor of \(y\), and the score moves from \(\mathrm{PMI}\) towards \(\pm 1\):

PMI \(P(y \mid x) = 0\) \(0.5\) \(0.9\) \(1\) 5.0 5.000 2.236 1.175 1.000 2.0 2.000 1.414 1.072 1.000 0.5 0.500 0.707 0.933 1.000 −2.0 −2.000 −1.414 −1.072 −1.000

So:

  • Weak prediction (\(P(y \mid x)\) near 0): the score is close to the PMI.
  • Deterministic prediction (\(P(y \mid x) = 1\)): the score is \(\pm 1\) whatever the PMI. (If the PMI is exactly 0 as well, which requires \(y\) to be the only symbol observed, the result is \(0^0 = 1\).)
  • In between, \(|T|\) always lies between \(|\mathrm{PMI}|\) and 1. For \(|\mathrm{PMI}| > 1\) the score decreases towards 1 as the conditional probability rises; for \(|\mathrm{PMI}| < 1\) it increases towards 1.
  • The sign is that of the PMI: positive when the pair co-occurs more often than independence predicts, negative when less often.

A score above 1 in absolute value therefore requires both \(|\mathrm{PMI}| > 1\) and an imperfect conditional probability, and values near \(\pm 1\) can come from a near-deterministic association or from a PMI near \(\pm 1\). The score is not a monotone measure of predictive strength. To rank pairs by how well one symbol predicts the other, use mle() or theil_u() alongside it.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These values come from ASymCat itself:

>>> from asymcat import CatScorer
>>> pairs = [("x", "a")] * 3 + [("y", "a")] + [("y", "b")] * 20 + [("z", "b")] * 10 + [("z", "c")] * 10
>>> scorer = CatScorer(pairs)
>>> scorer.mle()[("x", "a")]  # x always gives a; a comes from x 3 times in 4
(1.0, 0.75)
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.pmi()[("x", "a")]]
[2.398, 2.398]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.tresoldi()[("x", "a")]]
[1.0, 1.244]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.tresoldi()[("y", "b")]]
[0.949, 0.694]
>>> [round(v, 3) for v in scorer.tresoldi()[("y", "a")]]
[-0.66, -0.721]
  • ("x", "a"): \(x\) always occurs with \(a\), so \(T(x \to a) = 1\). In the other direction, \(P(x \mid a) = 0.75\) leaves part of the PMI: \(2.398^{0.25} = 1.244\). The deterministic direction gets the lower score, because the PMI exceeds 1.
  • ("y", "b"): \(P(b \mid y) = 0.952\), \(P(y \mid b) = 0.667\) and \(\mathrm{PMI} = 0.334\). Here the PMI is below 1, so the more predictive direction scores higher: \((0.949, 0.694)\).
  • ("y", "a"): the pair co-occurs less often than independence predicts (\(\mathrm{PMI} = -0.647\)), and both scores are negative: \((-0.660, -0.721)\).

docs.title: Significance and uncertainty
docs.text:
The resampling tools accept "tresoldi" like any other measure:

>>> pvalues = scorer.permutation_pvalue("tresoldi", n_permutations=999, seed=0)
>>> round(pvalues[("x", "a")][0], 2)
0.26
>>> intervals = scorer.bootstrap_ci("tresoldi", n_bootstrap=999, seed=0)
>>> len(intervals[("x", "a")])  # (low, high) for each direction
2

The saturation at \(\pm 1\) carries over to these tests. In the example above, the deterministic direction \(x \to a\) has a permutation p-value of 0.26. Shuffled data often produce scores of 1 or more, so a perfect association does not stand out. Test the conditional probability or Theil's U when the question is whether one symbol predicts another.

docs.title: Relation to other measures
docs.text: Measure Direction Range What it reports pmi symmetric \((-\infty, \infty)\) departure of the pair from independence mle directional \([0, 1]\) conditional probability of one symbol given the other theil_u directional \([0, 1]\) share of the uncertainty about one variable removed by the other tresoldi directional \((-\infty, \infty)\) PMI pulled towards \(\pm 1\) by the conditional probability

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Not normalized. The scale depends on the base rates in the data. Compare scores within a dataset rather than across datasets.
  • Rare pairs. PMI is unstable for low counts, and the exponent does not account for sample size. Use the resampling tools above to judge reliability.
  • Association, not causation. The direction refers to which conditional probability is used, not to temporal or causal order.

docs.title: tresoldi
docs.text:
tresoldi() -> dict[tuple[Any, Any], tuple[float, float]]

Return a Tresoldi scorer, the measure ASymCat provides for alignments.

For every pair (x, y) the tuple is (T(x→y), T(y→x)), with T(x→y) = sign(PMI) * |PMI(x, y)| ** (1 - P(y|x)): the PMI pulled towards ±1 as the conditional probability approaches 1. The conditional probabilities come from mle (so smoothing applies to them) and the PMI from pmi. See the documentation page "The Tresoldi measure" for its properties.

Returns:

Type Description Dict[Tuple[Any, Any], Tuple[float, float]]

Dictionary mapping symbol pairs to (T(x→y), T(y→x)) tuples.
